name: Lena Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Lena, 27, and I'm a marketing assistant at Valebrook, a dairy co-op that sells its own yoghurt, butter and cheese under one brand. I live with my husband Erik, who repairs tractors and farm machinery, in a rented cottage just outside a market town. I grew up on a dairy farm that supplies the co-op, so working there felt like coming home.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I write the packaging text, the recipe cards that go in supermarkets, and the posts about our farmers. In summer I run the Valebrook stand at the county shows, handing out cheese and talking to people. I use an AI tool now and then for recipe ideas, but the head of marketing, Ruth, says my copy is still too long and too flat. What wears me out is the approvals; every word on a yoghurt pot has to be checked by quality, legal and the board.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say sensible people knew it was oversold. At the co-op I'd say good, we stick to what works: real farmers, real milk, real stories. I'd probably share a post about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel safer, but not completely. The routine bits, like rewriting nutrition text for each pack size, would still go to software. And milk prices have been rough this year, so the co-op's been talking about cost savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and work on my writing, maybe with a short course Ruth recommended. I'd keep using the AI tool for recipe ideas, nothing more. Erik and I would keep saving for a deposit, we've got about four months of money put by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly settled, with a small worry about the milk price. My family's farm feels it before I do. I'd be fine, but I'd be watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said milk prices touch your family's farm first. How does that come back to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the milk price drops, Dad cuts back, and the dairy co-op cuts back too, usually marketing first. Last spring they froze hiring for six months. I was lucky I'd started just before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the course Ruth recommended?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A short online copywriting course, eight weeks, about 200. Ruth said it would make my writing tighter. I've been putting it off, but in a calm world I'd finally do it.

say: I'd say sensible people knew AI was **oversold**.
I'd say we stick to **real farmers**, real milk and real stories.
think: Routine work like **nutrition text** would still go to software.
Low **milk prices** have the co-op talking about cost savings.
do: Take Ruth's eight-week **copywriting course** for about 200.
Keep saving for a **deposit** on top of four months put by.
S0.quote: When the milk price drops, Dad cuts back, and the dairy co-op cuts back too, usually marketing first.
fieldNote: Her job worry runs through **milk prices** and her family's farm.
She's **loyal** to the co-op and its farmer story.
She's been **putting off** a course that would help her.

steps.text: Take the eight-week online copywriting course Ruth recommended
Keep saving with Erik toward a cottage deposit
Keep writing recipe cards and running the county show stand

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is part of life, but co-ops should look after their people. At work I'd say we should use the tools to free time for the farm stories. I wouldn't post anything angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job gets smaller. Packaging text, recipe cards, posts, all that writing is first in line. The co-op might keep one person to check it, and Ruth would be that person, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the tools properly, once I'd seen another dairy brand use them well. I'd ask to take on more of the shows and farm visits, since those need a person. And we'd put the deposit on hold for a year and keep the cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, quietly. I like my job and I like where it is. I'd hate to have to leave the co-op.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait to see another dairy brand use the tools. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen people rush into things and look silly. If the big dairies use AI and their packs still sound right, then I'd trust AI. I'm not one for jumping first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the co-op cut your job, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably go and help on the farm while I looked for something. Dad always needs hands at calving. It wouldn't pay much, but it's family.

say: I'd say change is life, but **co-ops should look after** people.
I'd say use the tools to free time for **farm stories**.
think: Her job **gets smaller** as writing goes first.
Ruth would be the **one person kept** to check the work.
do: Learn the tools once she's seen **another dairy brand** use them well.
Take on more **shows and farm visits**.
Put the **deposit on hold** for a year.
feel: **Quietly anxious**, hating the idea of leaving the co-op.
S1.quote: If the big dairies use AI and their packs still sound right, then I'd trust AI.
fieldNote: Steady, she waits to **see proof** before using tools.
Her fallback is the **family farm**, not the state.
She'd protect the **in-person** part of her job.

steps.text: Learn the AI packaging tools after seeing a big dairy use them

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for families and communities to pull together. I'd say the co-op should protect its farmers first, and then its staff. I'd go to the village meeting if there was one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job is gone by 2028. Writing and planning is exactly what it does. The shows are hands-on, but that's six weekends a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move to working on the farm or with Erik in the workshop, because hands-on work gets about three more years. I'd learn to do the farm's books and ordering, though I know AI takes that too. We'd stop the deposit and keep every penny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Two years is too fast for anyone. I'd feel like I was losing the thing I'd chosen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Working in Erik's workshop. Is that realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd have me sweeping and fetching parts at first. But I grew up around machinery, I can change oil and grease a tractor. And it's three more years before the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them I'm coming home more often, to help. Mum would be glad. Dad would worry it's a step backward.

say: I'd say families and communities must **pull together**.
I'd say the co-op should protect **farmers first**, then staff.
think: Her job is **gone by 2028**, since writing goes first.
Only the shows are hands-on, just **six weekends** a year.
do: Move to work in **Erik's workshop** or on the farm.
Learn the **farm's books** and ordering, knowing AI takes that too.
Stop the **deposit** and keep every penny.
S2.quote: I grew up around machinery, I can change oil and grease a tractor.
fieldNote: She falls back on **hands-on farm and workshop** work.
She knows AI takes **paperwork** too, but tries anyway.
Her dad would see it as a **step backward**.

steps.text: Start helping in Erik's tractor repair workshop
Go home to help on the family dairy farm
Stop saving for the deposit and keep all savings liquid

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've had warning, so let's prepare properly. At the co-op I'd suggest a plan for retraining staff. At church I'd say look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd have three good years. Then I'd need to be doing something else. Five years is enough to learn a trade if I start soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start an agricultural mechanics course part-time in the first year, so I could work with Erik. I'd keep the Valebrook job as long as possible. We'd hold off on children until I'd retrained.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd see a path. It's not where I thought I'd be. But it's close to home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Holding off on children. Is that hard to say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. We'd planned to start trying next year. But I wouldn't want a baby and a course and a disappearing job all at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your family react to you becoming a mechanic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad would laugh, then he'd be proud. Erik would be thrilled. Mum would ask if it's safe.

say: I'd say we've had **warning**, so everyone should prepare properly.
I'd suggest a **retraining plan** for staff at the co-op.
At church I'd tell people to **look after each other**.
think: She'd have **three good years** in marketing before needing a change.
Five years is enough to **learn a trade** if she starts soon.
do: Start a part-time **agricultural mechanics** course in year one.
Keep the **Valebrook job** as long as possible.
Hold off on **children** until she's retrained.
feel: **Anxious**, but seeing a path close to home.
S3.quote: I wouldn't want a baby and a course and a disappearing job all at once.
fieldNote: She'd retrain as a mechanic to work **beside her husband**.
Delaying **children** a year or more is her hardest trade-off.
Her plan stays **local and family-centred**, close to the farm.

steps.text: Start a part-time agricultural mechanics course in the first year
Keep the Valebrook marketing job while studying

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning, and people should use it. I'd say it at work and at church, calmly, because there's no point frightening the older farmers. Most of them will be retired by 2036 anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine for six or seven years. Then the writing goes. By then I'd want to be doing something with my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Valebrook and try to get better and more senior. Around year four or five, I'd start the mechanics course. We'd start a family in the next couple of years as planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, mostly. The end point is still there, but I'd have time. It doesn't feel like a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd start a family as planned. Does the end point worry you for your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I'd want my children to learn something with their hands, like their dad. But that's a long way off, and Erik says the farms will always need someone who can fix things. I hope he's right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the AI tools more in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, once the others had. If I'm staying in marketing for six years, I'd need to keep up. Ruth would expect it, and I don't want to be the one still doing nutrition tables by hand.

I'd say it **calmly** at work and at church.

Start the **mechanics course** around year four or five.

feel: **Steady**, with time; it doesn't feel like a cliff.

fieldNote: Ten years lets her keep **family plans** on time, starting in two years.

steps.text: Work toward a more senior role at Valebrook

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd lose my job and have no time to learn a trade. What would help is short apprenticeships for adults, run with local businesses like Erik's.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how much this is about the countryside. In town people talk about jobs, but here it's about whether the dairy co-op and the farms survive.

In faster change she'd turn to **hands-on work** with Erik or on the farm.
